case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative obligation on a State to protect a child from violence by a private actor, even where the agency knew of the danger, absent a custodial relationship that limits the child's freedom to act on his own behalf.
key_cases.relevance: This is the governing federal rule limiting constitutional liability when a child known to the agency is killed or seriously injured by a parent.
key_cases.quote: But nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors.

key_cases.case_name: Doe ex rel. Johnson v. South Carolina Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit recognized that a child involuntarily removed from her home has a substantive due process right not to be placed in a known, dangerous foster care environment in deliberate indifference to her safety, but held the caseworker entitled to qualified immunity because that right was not clearly established at the time.
key_cases.relevance: It is the governing circuit authority on agency liability for serious harm suffered by a child while under state supervision.
key_cases.quote: had a corresponding duty to refrain from placing her in a known, dangerous environment in deliberate indifference to her right to personal safety and security

key_cases.case_name: Adam Yafi v. Stafford Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(E), holding that where a parent is convicted of felony child abuse causing serious bodily injury to a sibling or subjects a child to aggravated circumstances, the Department need not prove it offered reasonable and appropriate rehabilitative services.
key_cases.relevance: It defines 'serious bodily injury' under Code § 16.1-283(E) as injury involving substantial risk of death, extreme pain, disfigurement or protracted loss of function.
key_cases.quote: the termination of Yafi’s residual parental rights under Code § 16.1-283(E)(iii) and 16.1-283(E)(iv) did not require a predicate showing that DSS provided any services to Yafi

key_cases.case_name: Dawn Farrell v. Warren County Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination of the mother's rights to all three children under Code § 16.1-283(B), holding that the statutory definitions of an abused or neglected child do not require proof of actual harm to each child and that abuse of a sibling plus an unsafe home environment supports the finding as to the others.
key_cases.relevance: It addresses serious non-fatal injury to an infant under circumstances the trial court found non-accidental.
key_cases.quote: Thus, we hold that the evidence was sufficient to support the trial court’s determination that E. and W. were abused or neglected.

key_cases.case_name: Kaywood v. Halifax County Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(B), holding that the three statutory prima facie triggers are not the only means of proving that the conditions causing the abuse cannot be corrected, and that whether correction is possible 'within a reasonable time' is judged from the context and attendant circumstances.
key_cases.relevance: The child had been seriously abused and injured to the point that his life was in danger, and the opinion shows how that degree of injury shapes the prospective judgment a Virginia court must make.
key_cases.quote: The phrase, “within a reasonable time” is not definable by any prescribed rule. Its meaning depends upon the context and the attendant circumstances; not upon mere opinion or expectation.
